Most of a mixture-of-experts model's parameters live inside its experts, and standard training keeps **every expert gradient resident in GPU memory** until the optimizer step. That memory scales with both the number and the size of the experts — exactly the two axes MoE architectures grow along. The constraint is not compute; it is holding the bookkeeping.

**Sonar-MoE**, posted to arXiv on 2 November, removes the constraint by updating each expert tensor *during* the backward pass and freeing its gradient the moment it is no longer needed. The GPU never holds more than one layer of expert gradients at a time.

## Numbers

The method is an engineering change, so the numbers are the argument. Fine-tuning **OLMoE-1B-7B** and **Granite 3.1-3B-A800M** in bf16 across **two expert-kernel backends**, Sonar-MoE:

- cuts **peak memory by 19–22%**
- takes **17–23% less time per step**
- produces **bitwise identical updates** to standard training when no expert gradient clipping is used
- keeps **held-out loss within 0.003** of every baseline

Bitwise identity is the detail that makes this more than a memory trick. The speedup and the memory saving are not bought with a change in optimization semantics — the gradients are numerically the same, so an existing training recipe reproduces exactly.

## The Catch Is Batching

The obvious implementation — updating one expert at a time as its gradient arrives — costs a **20–72% slowdown** at the same memory footprint. Sonar-MoE avoids that by updating **whole batched tensors rather than individual experts**, which keeps the fast path intact.

The result is a hybrid: it matches **optimizer-in-backward over all parameters** on both memory and speed, while still keeping the dense (non-expert) parameters on standard clipping. For anyone who wanted optimizer-in-backward for dense models but found it awkward to apply across a batched MoE parameter layout, this is the missing piece.

The practical upshot: MoE fine-tuning on a fixed GPU budget can now fit a larger expert configuration, and the wall-clock win is free. Both claims will need reproducing on other hardware and other expert kernels before they generalize beyond the two models and two backends tested here.

Paper: [arXiv:2611.03577](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03577)
